name: Lateral elbow tendinopathy

diagnosisContested.note: The clinical diagnosis is established, and history and physical examination are described as the gold standard. The underlying mechanism is less settled: the JOSPT guideline describes an interplay of tendon changes, motor control impairment and possible changes in pain processing. Several conditions can mimic it, including cervical radiculopathy, radial tunnel syndrome and posterior interosseous syndrome, so a self-reported label may be wrong.

avoidOrModify.movement: Loaded wrist extensor work at a load that aggravates symptoms
avoidOrModify.rationale: The guideline says applied loads should not exacerbate symptoms, and that loading should progress from isometric to isotonic to eccentric as tolerated. It also notes that no study described how load was determined or progressed. Sources disagree on the pain limit: Park 2010 used pain-free holds, Stasinopoulos 2017 allowed pain below 4 on VAS and stopped above 8, and the Bateman 2021 consensus allowed pain the patient deems acceptable. OPTimisE reported no related adverse events with the patient-acceptable rule, in a small sample not designed to detect harm. Sveinall 2024 lowered the weight next session if pain afterwards was not tolerable, affected sleep or lasted into the next session. No pain rule has been shown superior.

avoidOrModify.movement: Repeated wrist or elbow flexion and extension that aggravates symptoms, especially for long periods
avoidOrModify.rationale: Repetitive elbow or wrist flexion and extension for more than 2 hours a day is listed as a modifiable risk factor, and the guideline says aggravating repetitive motions should be minimized. A systematic review of work exposures reports repetitive movements over 2 hours a day with odds ratios of 2.8 to 4.7. This is association data. No RCT or systematic review testing activity modification alone was found.

avoidOrModify.movement: Repeated forearm twisting, rotating or screwing motions
avoidOrModify.rationale: Listed by the guideline as a modifiable risk factor. Risk-factor association only, with no trial showing that reducing it helps.

avoidOrModify.movement: Lifting objects with the forearm pronated (palm facing down)
avoidOrModify.rationale: The guideline says this should be minimized, in a narrative statement under ergonomics, and its ergonomics recommendation is grade E. Laboratory EMG supports the mechanism: ECRB activity during wrist extension was 72.3 %MVE pronated, 67.8 neutral and 54.6 supinated (pronation versus supination difference 17.8%, 95% CI 13.9 to 21.6), extensor activity during gripping was always greater with pronation, and adding a pull to a grip raised activity in all forearm muscles. These are isolated torque, dynamometer and push-pull tasks. No study found measured wrist extensor load during a gym lift, and no trial shows that a neutral or supinated grip reduces symptoms. Applying this to palm-down gym lifts such as reverse curls is an extrapolation made for this app.

avoidOrModify.movement: Handling very heavy loads in the hands
avoidOrModify.rationale: The guideline lists handling heavy tools over 20 kg as a modifiable risk factor. van Rijn 2009 reports handling loads over 20 kg at least 10 times a day (OR 2.6) and handling tools over 1 kg (ORs 2.1 to 3.0). This is occupational association data. Applying it to loaded carries or heavy barbell work is an extrapolation made for this app, and neither figure should be treated as a gym threshold.

avoidOrModify.movement: Isometric wrist extension or gripping above the individual pain threshold, especially when used for immediate pain relief
avoidOrModify.rationale: Isometric wrist extension (10 x 15 s) at a load 20% above pain threshold raised pain immediately and at 30 minutes compared with a load 20% below threshold, which matched control. Isometric gripping alone increased pain immediately compared with control. The evidence is acute and says nothing about long-term harm, and the app should not promise immediate relief from isometric holds.

avoidOrModify.movement: Isometric gripping that provokes lateral elbow pain
avoidOrModify.rationale: Reinstated in narrower form after the earlier verification removed an unsupported version. Isometric gripping increased pain immediately in Coombes 2025. In a very small case-control study, none of 11 participants reported pain at 15% of maximum voluntary grip and 6 of 11 reported mild discomfort at 30%. The grip intensity in Coombes 2025 was not read, so no source shows that harder or longer gripping is worse. Extending this to hangs or heavy carries is an extrapolation made for this app, and no study tested those tasks.

avoidOrModify.movement: Heavy slow resistance wrist extensor programs as an unsupervised home plan
avoidOrModify.rationale: In a feasibility trial using dumbbells as heavy as possible for 15 down to 6 repetitions, only 6 of 19 completed at least 30 of 36 sessions, eight named increased pain as the reason for non-compliance, and five reported increased pain as an adverse event. The authors concluded it was not suitable for patients with tennis elbow. A small pilot reported the opposite, but its groups differed in mean age by 14 years, so it is low confidence.

avoidOrModify.movement: Fast, forceful wrist extension with the wrist held in extreme radial or ulnar deviation
avoidOrModify.rationale: This is the laboratory authors' inference from isokinetic torque and EMG data, not an injury or symptom outcome.

candidateExercises.name: Wrist extension with a light dumbbell

dose.frequency: Once daily for 6-12 weeks. 3 x 15 for 6-12 weeks is the guideline's suggestion, without a weekly frequency. Once daily comes from Peterson 2011 (3 months) and the Bateman 2021 consensus (3 x 10-15).

candidateExercises.cautions: Load should not exacerbate symptoms. The best dose and load are unknown. Benefits are small: exercise beat passive care with low to very low certainty. Adding strengthening to education, stretching and activity modification improved nothing up to 52 weeks in McQueen 2021, and adding it to home stretching added nothing in Menta 2015. Not advised as a progression until an isometric version is tolerated, under the guideline's expert-opinion sequence.

alternativeDoses.load: Water container held in a clenched fist, forearm supported and pronated. Start 1 kg (women) or 2 kg (men), add 0.1 kg per week.
alternativeDoses.painRule: Told the condition was painful but harmless
alternativeDoses.note: Versus wait-list: lower pain during maximal contraction (p=0.0005). No difference in strength (p=0.17), DASH (p=0.30) or quality of life. 93% fully adhered.
Agreed by vote, not efficacy data. Applies to concentric and eccentric work.

alternativeDoses.protocol: Sveinall 2024 heavy slow resistance, not recommended here
alternativeDoses.frequency: 3 times a week with at least 48 h between sessions, 12 weeks
alternativeDoses.load: As heavy as possible within the repetitions, 4 s up and 4 s down, 2-3 min rest
alternativeDoses.painRule: Pain during training allowed. Reduce weight if pain afterwards is not tolerable, affects sleep or lasts into the next session.
alternativeDoses.note: Only 6 of 19 reached adequate adherence. Authors judged it unsuitable.

candidateExercises.name: Isometric wrist extension hold

dose.frequency: Once daily. From the Bateman 2021 consensus. Its results say 'up to 60 s', so 60 is a ceiling, and it is the only dose in this record set by a consensus process for routine treatment. The duration of the program is not set by the consensus; the isometric trial ran 8 weeks.

candidateExercises.cautions: No hold time has been shown to be better than another, and dose 'is based on clinical experience and varies among studies'. Load is unresolved: the Bateman 2021 discussion says maximal resistance, while the guideline starts at about 20%-40% MVIC and Coombes 2016 shows a flare above pain threshold. An app cannot measure these, so this record does not adopt maximal resistance; treat 60 s as a ceiling and reduce load or time if pain rises. Isometrics may raise pain at once, so do not promise immediate relief. In Vuvan 2020 PRTEE (SMD -0.92) and worst pain (SMD -0.80) improved versus wait-and-see, but global success and pain-free grip did not, and the authors doubt it works as a sole treatment. OPTimisE, an unpowered pilot that tested the package containing this dose, showed improvement similar to usual physiotherapy, and its delivered hold time is in a handbook that was not opened. The Vuvan trial used a water container as resistance; Park 2010 was equipment-free. Bateman 2021 attributes the 60 s dose to Barratt 2018, an uncontrolled service audit whose abstract gives no hold time and describes patient-specific high load into discomfort or pain.

alternativeDoses.frequency: Single bout, not a training frequency
alternativeDoses.note: Lowest-provocation dose found: comparable to control, with no flare and no relief. Acute only, so no treatment effect is shown. The same dose 20% above threshold raised pain for 30 minutes.

alternativeDoses.load: Patient-specific high load, then progressing to slow combined concentric and eccentric work
alternativeDoses.note: Named by Bateman 2021 as the origin of maximal resistance, 60 s, five repetitions. The abstract gives no hold time and the full text could not be opened, so that attribution is unconfirmed. Uncontrolled audit (n=182): responders 8% higher and treatments 42% fewer in phase three than phase one.

Lower pain at 1 month than delayed exercise (p<0.01), with no difference at 3, 6 or 12 months and no untreated control. That is 2000 s of holds a day (this record's arithmetic). Compliance fell to about 0.4 at 6 months, and Bateman 2021 rejected it as too burdensome.

alternativeDoses.frequency: Daily per the editorial; 5 treatments a week for 4 weeks per the trial abstract
alternativeDoses.load: Wrist in dorsal flexion; load not stated
alternativeDoses.painRule: Continue with mild pain (below 4 on VAS), stop if disabling (above 8 on VAS)
alternativeDoses.note: Secondary report, not read in the trial itself. Unusually high and confounded: the combined arm had 56 min of loading a session against 22 min. Part of a program with eccentric-concentric work, not tested alone.

alternativeDoses.load: RPE 9-12 in week 1, up to RPE 16 from week 4 if no pain. Same protocol in both arms; the experimental arm added a blood flow restriction cuff at 40-50% arterial occlusion pressure
alternativeDoses.note: Hold template only, covering wrist extensors among other muscle groups. n=20 completed. No between-group difference in pain.

alternativeDoses.load: 20% rising to 35% of maximum voluntary contraction, per secondary reports; water container with a handle per the guideline table
alternativeDoses.note: Hold time and sets were not available. Do not infer them. Bateman 2021 judged this load scheme too complicated.

alternativeDoses.load: Cited expert phases: pain-free contractions at about 20%-40% MVIC to start, above 40% MVIC later
alternativeDoses.note: Written for repetitions with no hold time, so it cannot be converted into seconds without inference.

candidateExercises.name: Eccentric wrist extension with a rubber bar

dose.frequency: Daily for 7 weeks in the Tyler 2010 trial, as tabulated by Yoon 2021.

candidateExercises.cautions: Requires a rubber bar. Tyler 2010 confirms the bar and about 7 weeks, but its abstract gives no sets or repetitions, so 3 x 15 rests on the table in Yoon 2021. Large gains in Tyler 2010 (DASH 76% vs 13%) come from 21 people. Pooled short-term effects are large with wide intervals (pain 1.12, CI 0.31 to 1.93), long-term results are inconclusive, and against concentric or isotonic work the pain benefit is small (SMD -0.30) with no difference in strength or function. Lapner 2022 found an eccentric program no better than no active treatment, and Wen 2011 was null. Progress only as tolerated without exacerbating symptoms.

alternativeDoses.load: Maximum load tolerated, applied by the other hand rather than a rubber bar, pushing the wrist from extended to fully flexed over 6-8 s (a tempo, not a hold)
alternativeDoses.painRule: Warned it would be quite painful
alternativeDoses.note: No difference from stretching and modalities at any point through 20 weeks.

alternativeDoses.load: Thera-Band progression across six exercises for elbow, wrist and shoulder
alternativeDoses.note: Astym beat this arm on DASH and grip at 4 weeks. No adverse effects in either group.
Yoon 2021 says 2 or 3 sets of 10 or 15 repetitions were common.

candidateExercises.name: Shoulder and scapular stabilizer training

dose.frequency: Not established in the sources opened.

candidateExercises.cautions: Grade C, only when impairments have been identified, and alongside wrist extensor strengthening. An app cannot identify those impairments, and the guideline passage reviewed names no specific exercises, so this does not justify mapping to a catalog exercise. The trials conflict: Mostafaee 2020 favored adding it, while Day 2021 found no added value in a multimodal program. The Bateman 2021 consensus also included shoulder girdle exercises (80% vote) without a dose in the passages read.

candidateExercises.name: Wrist extensor stretch

dose.frequency: Three 30 s holds before and three after loading exercises, with the once-daily program. From the Bateman 2021 consensus.

alternativeDoses.frequency: Three holds before and three after eccentric exercise each session, with 30 s rest between
alternativeDoses.note: A recommendation, not trial data, and the source of the common dose.
Given to both arms of a forearm band trial, so stretching itself was not tested.

alternativeDoses.load: Straight elbow, pronated forearm, palmar-flexed wrist
alternativeDoses.note: Exact position is the most specific found.

alternativeDoses.painRule: To the point of pull, not pain
alternativeDoses.note: Same volume as Nishizuka 2017. Strengthening in this trial was separate, at 2 sessions a week.

candidateExercises.cautions: Reinstated: the earlier verification removed it because no opened source gave a dose, and Bateman 2021 and others now do. The dose was chosen by vote for practicality (80% on second vote). No source isolates a benefit: 'the relative effectiveness of stretching vs strengthening for the wrist extensors remains unknown', and no trial here compares stretching with no stretching. Catalog: no forearm stretch id was found in a search of the app's workout-guide assets, so it is marked new.

redFlags.sign: Atypical mass or swelling around the elbow
redFlags.action: Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.
Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.
Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.

redFlags.sign: Feeling systemically unwell, malaise or weight loss alongside elbow symptoms
redFlags.action: Stop elbow-loading exercise and seek urgent medical assessment.

redFlags.sign: Progressive weakness when extending the fingers or wrist
redFlags.action: Stop loading the arm and get prompt medical assessment. This can point to posterior interosseous nerve compression. The source sets no timing, so 'prompt' is this report's wording.

redFlags.sign: Symptoms that may come from another condition, such as the neck or a nerve entrapment, or that do not fit the usual pattern
redFlags.action: Get a professional evaluation. The guideline says therapists should identify conditions that mimic this one and promptly refer when appropriate. It lists the conditions but not patient-facing signs, so the wording here is this report's own. Trial exclusions show which presentations are untested in this evidence: recent significant trauma, inflammatory arthritis or gout, elbow osteoarthritis, neurological symptoms at onset, and neck pain and stiffness starting at a similar time.

redFlags.sign: No improvement after 12-24 weeks of treatment
redFlags.action: Not urgent. Get a clinical review. The BESS pathway treats failure to improve within 12-24 weeks as a trigger for secondary care referral.

limitations: Overall grade stays low. The Cochrane review (Wallis 2024) rates manual therapy and exercise evidence low certainty with benefits that may not be clinically worthwhile, and Karanasios 2021 rates its comparisons low to very low certainty. Evidence for any specific isometric hold time is lower still: it rests on consensus, one small trial without an untreated control, an acute experiment and a secondary report. CONTRADICTIONS. (1) Whether to recommend exercise: Lucado 2022 gives it grade B and Singh 2023 a strong recommendation for physiotherapy, while Lapner 2022 (strong, moderate) says eccentric programs are similar to no active treatment and does not support exercise-based physiotherapy. Lapner excluded combination therapies and rated the pain evidence low. (2) Pain during exercise: Lucado 2022 says loads should not exacerbate symptoms and Park 2010 used pain-free holds; Bateman 2021 allows patient-acceptable pain, Stasinopoulos allows below 4 on VAS, and Wen 2011 warned the work would be quite painful. (3) Isometric analgesia: Coombes 2016, Coombes 2025 and the review by Clifford 2020 do not support immediate relief. (4) Isometric hold wording: Bateman 2021 says 'up to 60 s' in its results and 'maximal resistance, held for 60 s' in its discussion, attributed to Barratt and Selfe 2018, an uncontrolled audit whose abstract gives no hold time and whose full text could not be opened. One searcher reported that Bateman 2021 lacks 'maximal resistance'; the full text was re-read and it is there. (5) Park 2010 says four sets of 50 daily. Bateman 2021 and Stasinopoulos 2022a restate it as 50 repetitions four times a day. The primary wording is used here. (6) Stasinopoulos 2017 is reported as daily by the editorial and 5 treatments a week by the abstract, and the 45 s x 15 dose was never read in the trial itself. (7) Vuvan 2020 global success is 29% vs 26% in its abstract, while Clifford 2020 reports overall improvement of 86% vs 63%. Both are non-significant, and the likely difference in threshold could not be confirmed without the full text. (8) Heavy loading: Sveinall 2024 found it unsuitable and Divya Mary 2025 reported it superior, the latter with failed-looking randomisation (mean age 48.42 vs 62.42) and an age table that does not sum to n. (9) Manual therapy: grade B in Lucado 2022, excluded by Bateman 2021 partly on cost and burden. (10) Bracing: Grade D and F in Lucado 2022, conditional in Singh 2023, included in Bateman 2021 (80%), null in Nishizuka 2017, inconclusive in Struijs 2002 and Dion 2017, short-term benefit in Ouyang 2026. Shahabi 2020 concludes bracing is reasonable, though every interval quoted includes zero. (11) Injections: Kinney 2023 reports PRP and autologous blood as most effective long term, while Karjalainen 2021 finds no clinically significant benefit over placebo at three months with moderate certainty. (12) Long term: physiotherapy advantages generally do not persist to one year (Bisset 2006, Smidt 2002, Coombes 2013, Chen Q 2023), so recovery cannot be separated from natural history (Leschinger 2022). (13) Adherence: 93% with light graded loads in Peterson 2011 and 32% with heavy loads in Sveinall 2024, but 71% of 104 studies report no adherence data (Taylor 2024). (14) Lucado 2022 lists tools over 20 kg as a risk factor, while van Rijn 2009 reports tools over 1 kg and loads over 20 kg. (15) Sveinall 2024 treats sleep-disturbing pain after training as a cue to reduce weight, while the NHS Highland pathway lists night pain as a red flag. This record keeps the red flag for night pain that is not explained by a recent session; that split is this record's reading. GAPS. No study found measured wrist extensor load during a gym lift, and 29 titles in that search were not screened. No trial tested activity modification alone. Vuvan 2020 hold time and sets remain unread, the OPTimisE handbook was not opened, and the Barratt 2018 protocol was not read. NICE CKS (HTTP 403), the German AWMF original (HTTP 500), the Dutch guideline (not located), the JOA recommendations (HTTP 403) and the ACOEM recommendations were not read; the BESS exercise sheets were not opened. Cochrane reviews were read as abstracts through PubMed or PMC, not through the Cochrane Library. Fragility is a concern: 8 of 29 significant outcomes in 17 nonoperative RCTs reversed with one event (Shah 2025). Do not reuse the Chen Q 2023 ESWT function interval, which appears misprinted. Coombes 2013 intervals are 99%. Red flags still come from one local NHS pathway and one case-based article, not a validated screening tool, and patient-facing wording is partly this record's own. Applying occupational and laboratory data to gym movements is an extrapolation. This is general information and not treatment or diagnosis.

valuesCorrected: Sevier 2015 stretch frequency: was tied to 2 sessions a week; the paper says 3 times daily, one 30 s repetition.
Park JH 2026: type changed from controlled_trial to rct, because the paper states randomisation. The cuff applies only to the experimental arm.
Barratt and Selfe: was reported as not found. It is Physiotherapy 2018;104(2):209-216, PMID 29366541, and was added as a source with abstract access.
Wen 2011: resistance comes from the other hand, not a rubber bar.
Martinez-Silvestrini 2005: load changed from not extracted to elastic resistance band, per the Yoon 2021 table.
Wallis 2024 table row: 23 trials and 1612 people is the whole review; the pain estimate comes from 12 trials and 1023 people.
Taylor 2024: 71% refers to 74 of 104 studies, not trials.
Lucado 2022 grade B row: only rigid taping is limited to irritable cases, and dry needling is not limited to short-term relief.
OPTimisE: changed from not better than usual physiotherapy to similar improvement in an unpowered pilot.
accessLevel for nhs_highland and cha2014 changed from not_reconfirmed to full_text, because both were opened and support their red flags.
unverifiable: Barratt 2018 hold time, repetitions and load: subscription article, repository copy returned 403. Bateman 2021 attribution of 60 s x 5 to it is unconfirmed.
Vuvan 2020 hold time, sets and pain rule: paywalled, repository copy returned 403.
Coombes 2025 grip intensity and Coombes 2016 load method: abstract only.
Stasinopoulos 2017 45 s x 15: read only through Stasinopoulos 2022a.
Tyler 2010 3 x 15: read only in the Yoon 2021 table.
Sources marked abstract_only were checked against their PubMed abstract only.
Singh 2023, Bisset 2006 and Kinney 2023 were checked through a summarising page fetch, because Europe PMC full-text XML returned HTTP 500.
Lucado 2022 was read from the orthopt.org PDF. The publisher copy returned 403 earlier. The PDF is text-extracted, so table layout may be imperfect.

Red flags: 'Stop elbow-loading exercise' is not in the NHS Highland pathway, whose action is an urgent call to on-call orthopaedics plus a referral. Cha 2014 names the digit extensors and extensor carpi radialis brevis, so 'wrist' is an anatomical reading.
